# Operations Runbook

## Automatic compaction

Available since v0.7.0. Install/update the same scope from the release archive and restart OpenCode
before using the new commands. No existing goal migration or default opt-in is required.

Use `/target context default 100k` for new sessions, or `/target context 70%` in the current session.
`/target context status` and `/target doctor` include the last context measurement, chosen model,
threshold, pending request, errors and recent events. Settings reside in `<state_dir>/context` and
survive `/target clear`; `context reset` copies the current defaults. `context off` preserves the
threshold and does not disable the host's own overflow compaction.

If the retained context is above the threshold immediately after a summary, increase the threshold.
If compaction fails three times, inspect the host error and resume explicitly once corrected.
If a request times out after two minutes or its result is unknown, Target stays active but waits
behind its durable request fence. It polls for the completed summary without repeating the compact;
an unknown result is recorded once rather than counted as repeated failures. Late completion wakes
the scheduler automatically, after the host becomes idle and pending input is resolved. History
reconciliation also works after restart. Settings toggles do not discard the pending operation.
If the host operation never completes, inspect its state/errors and use manual `/compact` to produce
a newer completed summary. A manually paused/stopped Target is never resumed by compaction.
Older installations may already have paused a Target on timeout: update, restart OpenCode and use
`/target resume` explicitly after confirming compaction completed. The fix does not undo old pauses.

## Confirm installation

Run `sh install.sh` or `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install.ps1` from the archive.
Node.js 22+ is required. Both plugins and TUI registration are installed in one step, with no
dependency installation or manual JSON editing. The generated installer bundles its JSONC parser.
`OPENCODE_CONFIG_DIR` overrides the destination, followed by `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`; otherwise the
global destination is `~/.config/opencode`. `OPENCODE_TUI_CONFIG` selects an explicit global TUI config file.
Both install and uninstall wrappers prompt for local/global scope. Use `--local --project-dir <path>`
or `--global` for Shell, and `-Local -ProjectDir <path>` or `-Global` for PowerShell to skip prompts.
Local plugins and TUI config live in `<project>/.opencode`; local state is `.opencode/target/state`.
`target/package.json` records installed version and state/config paths. Updates report old → new
archive versions and preserve goals. Stop OpenCode and run `uninstall.sh` / `uninstall.ps1` (or
Russian variants) with the same scope to remove plugins, registrations, metadata and scoped state.
Legacy global goals remain global; local removal does not delete them. Explicitly shared custom
state directories are removed when uninstalling an installation that uses them.

The indicator uses stock `session_prompt_right` (upstream 1.18.34). Installation, updates and
removal leave the OpenCode executable and unrelated extension metadata untouched. Existing
custom OpenCode installations are not migrated; reinstall stock OpenCode separately if desired.
Installer file/config changes are protected by `.target-install.lock` and rolled back on failure.

1. Confirm the server plugin file exists in one of OpenCode's plugin locations:

   ```text
   ~/.config/opencode/plugins/target.js
   .opencode/plugins/target.js
   ```

   On Windows, the equivalent user location is normally:

   ```text
   %USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode\plugins\target.js
   ```

2. The install scripts also copy the TUI plugin and automatically register it in the selected scope's
   `tui.json` or `tui.jsonc`. Confirm that `target.js` exists under the TUI plugin directory:

   ```text
   ~/.config/opencode/tui-plugins/target.js
   ```

   The resulting registration is equivalent to:

   ```json
   { "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/tui.json", "plugin": ["./tui-plugins/target.js"] }
   ```

3. Restart OpenCode. TUI and server plugins are loaded at startup.
4. Start a new session so the current tool list is loaded.
5. Run `/target help`; the indicator appears under the prompt when the session has a Target.

Repeated installation preserves existing configuration and tuple options and does not append
duplicate plugin entries. It re-enables only `opencode-target-tui` when disabled. If both
`tui.json` and `tui.jsonc` exist, registration goes into `tui.jsonc` while considering entries from
both. Config parse errors stop the installer with a nonzero exit; repair the indicated file and
rerun. A failed installation restores the previous plugin and config bytes.

Rerunning an installer replaces both plugin files with the archive's versions and reports an update.
To uninstall completely, stop OpenCode and use `sh install.sh --uninstall` or
`powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\install.ps1 -Uninstall`. This removes installed Target
files, Target entries from the selected JSON/JSONC server and TUI layers (plus an explicit TUI config),
installation metadata, and scoped saved Target state. Custom tuple `state_dir` paths are also removed;
global removal uses the recorded system state path. Local removal keeps legacy global state.
Configuration is validated before removal; unrelated plugin files and configuration are retained.

The TUI indicator is display-only. It polls the local state file and never performs lifecycle
transitions or state quarantine. A missing Target hides the indicator; an unreadable state shows
`Target · unavailable` until the next successful read.

The plugin state directory is separate from the plugin installation directory. See
`docs/state-format.md`.

## Inspect current state

Use the command inside the affected session:

```text
/target status
/target budget
/target doctor
```

The `get_target` model tool returns the same persisted state with root and descendant usage.
Runtime logs are written through `client.app.log` and use the `opencode-target` plugin identity.

`/target doctor` separately reports persisted state, the messages API, and the child-session API.
An API error is not interpreted as an empty response, because doing so could hide usage or
descendant-session data.

Completed Targets are terminal. If `/target pause`, `/target resume`, or another delayed control
operation is sent after completion, the command is rejected; start a new Target for a new
objective instead.

If state JSON is malformed, Target moves it to `<state_dir>/corrupt/` with a timestamp suffix and
raises a `TARGET_STATE_CORRUPT` diagnostic. Preserve that file before manual recovery.

## Target is not continuing

Check these in order:

1. `/target status` must report `active`.
2. Confirm `auto_continue` is not `false`.
3. Confirm the token budget has not reached `budget_limited`.
4. Check for `usage_limited`, `paused`, or `blocked` with `/target status`.
5. Check whether a control command intentionally deferred one continuation.
6. Inspect OpenCode logs for a runtime error or a continuation scheduling failure.
7. If the Target is paused or blocked, resolve the reason and run `/target resume`.

Host API calls have a bounded `host_api_timeout_ms` (30 seconds by default). A timeout is retried
according to `accounting_retry`; after the retry budget is exhausted, the active Target is paused
with a diagnostic stop reason instead of remaining indefinitely in an in-flight continuation.

Provider prompt failures follow the same fail-closed rule. Typed OpenCode prompt failures pause
the Target after bounded retries; unexpected continuation exceptions block it with a bounded
diagnostic reason. Neither path leaves an active Target eligible for an uncontrolled retry loop.

Prompt timeouts signal transport cancellation using the SDK's `AbortSignal`. Cancellation of
the request does not prove that OpenCode stopped its server-side turn. Until the original request
settles, Target refuses overlapping prompts and pauses with `OPENCODE_PROMPT_PENDING` rather than
retrying into an unknown running turn. The scheduler lease is released when this processing ends.
Check the `opencode-target` log entries `Target continuation prompt started`, `finished`, and
`failed`, including `sessionID`, `phase`, and error code. These entries do not include prompt text.
If the TUI cannot accept commands or Ctrl-C, restart OpenCode and inspect its logs before resuming.
The Orca status alone is not evidence that the session is making progress. Isolate server and TUI
plugins in a separate configuration to establish a conflict; no specific third-party conflict is
currently confirmed.

If an OpenCode process exits while owning continuation, its persisted scheduler lease becomes
recoverable after `scheduler_lease_ms` (30 seconds by default). A later `session.idle` event can
then acquire the expired lease. Do not place the state directory on a shared network filesystem;
the lock and lease guarantees target processes on one host with a shared local state directory.

Run configured verification gates explicitly with `/target verify` or `/target verify <gate-id>`.
Gate commands come from trusted plugin configuration and execute in the current project directory.
A failed gate leaves its linked requirement open.

Target also refreshes the Git fingerprint at idle and before model completion. If files changed
after a successful verification, `/target report` and `/target status` expose the resulting stale
or missing evidence and completion is rejected until the requirement is verified again.

Verification retry settings are `maxAttempts`, `baseDelayMs`, and `maxDelayMs`. Keep them bounded;
retries are intended for transient host/provider failures, not for ordinary test or lint failures.
Use `/target explain` to inspect the recorded attempt count.

Use `/target checkpoint [summary]` before a risky phase to save a manual metadata marker. This is
not a Git commit and does not provide automatic rollback. If a later verification reports stale
evidence, rerun the affected gate after the worktree reaches the intended state.

Do not mark a Target active by hand in JSON while a previous turn may still be finishing.

Runtime limits can be configured with `max_automatic_turns`, `max_active_seconds`, and
`max_no_progress_turns`. A reached limit produces `usage_limited` with a specific stop reason.
Changing token budget does not remove these limits; update configuration and explicitly resume only
after confirming the Target should continue.

For evidence-backed Targets, inspect `/target status` before completion. The status output shows
the number of verified requirements. A model must use `add_target_evidence` for each declared
requirement; a completion request with missing evidence is rejected and leaves the Target active.

## Budget limited

Budget exhaustion is a deterministic runtime transition:

```text
/target budget 300000
/target resume
```

Changing the budget alone does not resume a Target. Resume remains `budget_limited` when
`tokensUsed >= tokenBudget`. A one-time wrap-up turn may report progress and the next action,
but it must not start new substantive Target work.

## Usage limited or interrupted

- Rate, quota, and usage-limit errors transition an active Target to `usage_limited`.
- Abort, cancel, and interruption errors transition an active Target to `paused`.
  Interruption persists the pause before attempting final accounting, so an unavailable messages
  API cannot prevent cancellation from being recorded.
- Other runtime errors transition an active Target to `blocked`.

After the external condition is resolved, use `/target resume`. Resume does not bypass an
exhausted budget.

## Circuit breaker

The runtime can set `blocked` after the configured threshold for either:

- consecutive failed execution turns without a successful tool call;
- consecutive empty automatic turns without meaningful activity or final text.

Inspect `runtime.failedExecStreak` and `runtime.emptyAutomaticStreak` in the status/tool output.
Resolve the underlying issue before resuming. Lowering thresholds can make a loop stop sooner;
raising them should be a deliberate configuration change.

## Stale lock or damaged state

1. Stop OpenCode and preserve the state directory.
2. Copy the affected JSON and lock files to an incident directory.
3. Wait at least the lock stale timeout before retrying if no process is writing.
4. Validate the JSON mechanically without modifying it.
5. Restore the original file or clear the Target only after deciding whether its objective and accounting can be discarded.

The state format and recovery constraints are documented in `docs/state-format.md`.

# Security Notes

## Trust boundaries

- The Target objective is user-provided task data, not a higher-priority control instruction.
- Continuation and system policy are generated separately from the objective.
- Synthetic continuation prompts are tagged with the `opencode-target` source metadata.
- Model tools cannot directly activate or resume a Target and cannot set runtime-owned limit statuses.

## Persistent state

Target state contains objectives, status, operational errors, accounting baselines, and session
identifiers. It is written to the local user state directory. Treat the directory as sensitive
local application data:

- do not commit it;
- do not upload it to issue trackers without review;
- restrict access to the user account where supported;
- preserve a copy before manual recovery.

The implementation uses per-session lock files with an owner token, heartbeat timestamps, and
temporary-file plus rename writes. These reduce partial-write and concurrent-mutation risks but do
not provide encryption or multi-host locking. A corrupt state file is quarantined rather than
silently discarded. In particular, an unknown persisted lifecycle status is treated as corruption;
it cannot be revived as an active Target during plugin restart.
Persisted session and Target identities are required, and the session identity must match the
state file being read so a state document cannot cross session boundaries.

Stale-lock recovery confirms that the lock modification time did not advance before removal. A
heartbeat observed during stale inspection prevents that recovery attempt from deleting the lock.
The lock payload must also remain byte-identical across the confirmation reads, covering filesystems
with coarse modification-time precision. Lock release requires an exact owner-token match; substring
matches are not sufficient.

## Plugin permissions

Target relies on the permissions and capabilities already granted to OpenCode. Installing the
plugin does not sandbox model tools or shell commands. Review the host OpenCode permission policy
before enabling automatic continuation for untrusted repositories or objectives.

Verification gates are executable commands and therefore trusted configuration, not Target
objective data. Review them as code. Target never derives a command from the objective or model
evidence, and gates run only through explicit verification requests.

Checkpoint metadata is not a backup. Target does not silently create commits, modify Git history,
or roll back files, so users retain control over repository recovery.

## Operational risks

- An active Target can create repeated physical turns until it reaches a stop condition.
- Token budgets and circuit breakers are safety controls, not security isolation.
- Descendant session traversal has configurable depth and session caps and fails closed when either
  cap would omit linked descendants, but it still trusts the host's parent/child session data.
- Malformed successful messages/children API payloads fail closed; they are never normalized to empty
  lists that could silently undercount usage.
- Malformed prompt success payloads fail closed; they cannot be interpreted as an empty continuation
  and silently trigger another automatic turn.
- A compromised or modified plugin file executes with the same privileges as OpenCode.

Keep the plugin source and generated artifact reviewable, run `npm run check` before distribution,
and install only from a trusted project copy or package source.

# Persisted State Format

Accounting update: watermarks are no longer capped (`accounting.maxEntries: null`).
New states carry `accounting.tokenSemantics: "opencode-normalized-v1"`; absent markers
retain the legacy formula documented below. See [recovery](token-accounting-recovery.md)
for normalization, request records and explicit historical reconstruction.

Target stores one JSON document per OpenCode session. The file is selected by a URL-safe
base64 encoding of the session ID:

```text
Linux/macOS: ~/.local/state/opencode-target/targets/<encoded-session>.json
Windows:     %LOCALAPPDATA%\opencode-target\targets\<encoded-session>.json
```

The global default state directory can be overridden with `OPENCODE_TARGET_STATE_DIR`.
Automatic local installations instead use `<project>/.opencode/target/state`.
The installer records the selected state path, scope, version, custom TUI config path and owned
config files in `<config-dir>/target/package.json`. Both installed plugins resolve the same path
from this metadata; explicit plugin `state_dir` options take precedence. Updates retain the path.
Legacy shared state remains global; local installation does not copy or delete those goals.
Manually copied plugins without installation metadata keep the defaults above.

Malformed or schema-invalid state is never treated as an absent Target. The runtime atomically
moves it to `<state_dir>/corrupt/<original>.<timestamp>.<id>.corrupt` and reports
`TARGET_STATE_CORRUPT` so an operator can inspect or restore it explicitly.

The persistence implementation uses a dedicated `TargetStore`; this does not change the on-disk
directory layout or the public lifecycle API.

Writes are atomic: state is written to a per-process temporary file and moved into place with
`rename`. On Windows, `rename` can transiently fail with `EPERM`, `EACCES`, or `EBUSY` while
another handle still has the destination open. `TargetStore` retries those codes with bounded
exponential backoff, and uses the same retry for quarantine moves. Non-transient filesystem
errors still fail immediately and are surfaced to the caller.

## Context settings and request state

Automatic `/compact` uses an independent version `1` document store in `<state_dir>/context`.
It reuses `TargetStore` atomic writes, locks and corruption quarantine. Documents live under
`context/targets/<base64url-key>.json`, with keys `defaults` and `session:<OpenCode-session-id>`.
These are context records, not Target goals; the separate namespace prevents goal traversal or
the TUI from treating them as lifecycle files. Clearing a goal leaves these settings intact.

Each document has `version`, `sessionID` (the storage key), `settings: { enabled, threshold }`,
and `runtime`. Threshold is null or `{ kind: "tokens" | "percent", value: positive integer }`;
percent is limited to 1–99. Session records also have `source` and a monotonically increasing
settings `revision`. Missing records start disabled and snapshot defaults on first use.

Session `runtime` contains the last sample/model/window/threshold, summary ID, last completion/error,
arming state, bounded retry state, and up to 50 diagnostic events. `pending` is null or a request
with ID, expected `targetID`, start time, previous summary ID and settings revision. It is written
before the API call and survives restart. An uncertain result preserves `pending` until a newer
completed summary is observed. A settings command rearms the threshold but never erases that fence.
An optional `pending.uncertainAtMs` records the first timeout/unknown-result observation; it keeps
the request fenced without pausing the Target or increasing `failureAttempts`. The corresponding
`compaction.uncertain` event is emitted once per request. Older records without this marker remain
readable. Only confirmed request failures count toward the three-failure pause policy.
Old Target schemas require no migration; context records are independent and initially absent.

## Schema

The current persisted schema version is `3`. The implementation normalizes loaded state to the
current shape before using it. Unknown status values are schema corruption: they are quarantined
and never silently revived as `active` after restart. `sessionID` and `targetID` are required
identity fields; the stored `sessionID` must also match the session file being read.

Schema versions `2` and `3` are supported. Version `2` is normalized to the current version when
the state is next written. Missing, older, non-integer, and future schema versions are quarantined
instead of being interpreted with guessed semantics.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `version` | number | Current schema version, currently `3`. |
| `sessionID` | string | Root OpenCode session owning the Target. |
| `targetID` | string | Unique logical Target generation. Used by stale-write guards. |
| `objective` | string | User-provided objective, normalized and limited to 4000 characters. |
| `status` | string | One of `active`, `paused`, `blocked`, `usage_limited`, `budget_limited`, `complete`. |
| `tokenBudget` | positive integer or null | Target token limit, or unbounded when null. |
| `tokensUsed` | integer | Combined root and descendant billable tokens. |
| `rootTokensUsed` | integer | Billable tokens from the root session. |
| `descendantTokensUsed` | integer | Billable tokens from linked child sessions. |
| `timeUsedSeconds` | integer | Active Target wall-clock time in seconds. |
| `createdAtMs` | number | Target creation timestamp in milliseconds. |
| `updatedAtMs` | number | Last persisted update timestamp. |
| `lastStatusChangeAtMs` | number | Timestamp of the latest lifecycle status change. |
| `activeStartedAtMs` | number or null | Start of the current active interval. |
| `accumulatedActiveMs` | number | Completed active intervals in milliseconds. |
| `continuationCount` | integer | Number of automatic continuation turns started. |
| `schedulerLease` | object or null | Current continuation owner, acquisition time, and expiry. Only the matching owner may renew, release, or start the leased turn. |
| `limits` | object | Persisted runtime limits: `maxAutomaticTurns`, `maxActiveSeconds`, and `maxNoProgressTurns`; each is a positive integer or null. |
| `requirements` | array | Declared acceptance requirements. Each item has an `id`, `text`, `status`, and bounded evidence list. |
| `verification` | array | Trusted configured gates with `id`, `command`, optional `requirementID`, and bounded retry policy. |
| `evidenceFingerprint` | string or null | Last worktree fingerprint associated with evidence. A changed fingerprint invalidates prior evidence. |
| `journal` | array | Bounded lifecycle decision history, limited to the most recent 200 events. |
| `checkpoints` | array | Bounded manual checkpoint metadata; checkpoints never create commits or perform rollback. |
| `verificationSummary` | object | Report-only aggregate of persisted verification events: total, passed, failed, and attempts. |
| `accounting` | object | Watermark completeness metadata: tracked messages, entry cap, and whether history was truncated. |
| `continuationDeferrals` | integer | Pending one-shot deferrals from control commands. |
| `lastContinuationAtMs` | number or null | Timestamp of the latest continuation start. |
| `lastError` | string or null | Latest runtime error, when present. |
| `stopReason` | string or null | Reason the Target was stopped or blocked. |
| `budgetWrapupSent` | boolean | Whether the one-time budget wrap-up turn was sent. |
| `usageByMessage` | object | Cumulative per-message accounting baselines keyed by `sessionID:messageID`. |
| `runtime` | object | Breaker streaks, evaluated assistant IDs, and latest turn classification. |

`runtime.evaluatedThroughMs` is the completed-message watermark; the bounded recent ID list
deduplicates messages at its boundary. `runtime.pendingAutomaticAtMs` marks an automatic dispatch
whose result is not classified yet. Missing fields normalize to zero/null in schemas 2 and 3.

## Accounting fields

For an assistant message, billable usage is:

```text
max(0, input - cache.read) + output
```

Plan-mode messages are excluded. `usageByMessage` stores the largest observed cumulative value
for each message. Later observations charge only the positive delta, which prevents duplicate
charges when OpenCode exposes partial or streaming token metadata.

For a message whose creation timestamp predates the Target, the first observation is a baseline
even if OpenCode did not expose it during activation. Its current cumulative value is stored without
charge; future positive deltas remain billable.

The map is bounded by the implementation to prevent unbounded state-file growth.
At Target creation, the complete pre-Target snapshot is installed in `usageByMessage` in the same
locked write as the new active state. Creation is rejected with `TARGET_BASELINE_TOO_LARGE` if
that snapshot cannot fit the watermark capacity; no partial Target file is written.

## Safe recovery

- Do not change `targetID` manually while a session may still have callbacks in flight.
- Prefer `/target pause`, `/target budget`, `/target resume`, or `/target clear` over editing JSON.
- Stop OpenCode before moving or archiving state files.
- If a state file is malformed, preserve a copy for diagnosis and use `/target clear` only after confirming that the Target can be discarded.
- A stale lock can normally be recovered automatically after the 15-second stale threshold. Lock
  acquisition waits long enough to cross that threshold before timing out. Do not delete a lock
  while another OpenCode process may still be writing.

There is no general-purpose migration command. Schema changes must be implemented in
`normalizeTarget`, covered by tests, and documented here before release.

# Token accounting recovery

The former 12,000-entry watermark cap evicted deduplication identities while retaining
their charges. Full-history continuation scans charged evicted records again. The fix
retains all identities through accounting, normalization, baseline seeding and restart.
`accounting.maxEntries` is now null; historical `truncated: true` remains sticky.

New Targets persist `accounting.tokenSemantics: "opencode-normalized-v1"` and count
`input + cache.write + output + reasoning`: OpenCode already separates cache reads
from input and reasoning from output. States without this marker retain the legacy
formula until explicit reconstruction, avoiding false deltas against old watermarks.
Distinct step-finish IDs identify recorded requests, including paid retries. Their sum
replaces, rather than supplements, the message's latest-request snapshot.

An anonymized live state snapshot contained 2,350,740,149 tokens and 12,000 watermarks,
with truncated=true. Independent unique-message, step-finish and message-event
high-watermark sums agreed on 532,549,680 under the legacy formula (excess:
1,818,190,469). The normalized formula yielded 645,688,912. These are diagnostic
snapshots, not replacement values for a subsequently changed Target.

## Explicit historical reconstruction

1. Install the fixed plugin and restart OpenCode: an already loaded old plugin still
   evicts watermarks. Coordinate a quiet accounting boundary and back up Target JSON.
2. Read a consistent, read-only host database snapshot: linked sessions, message usage,
   unique step-finish parts and necessary usage events. Never export prompts or secrets.
3. Verify completeness, plan exclusions, activation time and actual activation baseline.
   Requests straddling activation need the real baseline, not a guessed proportional split.
   Compare message totals with request totals and report missing records.
4. Produce a dry-run root/descendant report. Missing usage or activation baselines make
   exact reconstruction impossible: explicitly report the unknown boundary. A partial sum
   must not be labeled exact; retries without saved usage must not be assigned invented tokens.
5. After explicit approval, hold the session lock, recheck target ID and state/source
   freshness, and atomically replace totals AND complete watermarks using the documented
   formula and its semantics marker. Clear truncation only after proving completeness.
   Preserve lifecycle status, budget, objective and all other Target metadata.
6. Replay the identical source snapshot: delta must be zero. Verify context and TUI
   against the same saved total before allowing further accounting.

No existing Target was modified or reset during this investigation. Reconstruction is
manual; the plugin does not silently rewrite historical totals on load.

# Writing Good Tests

**Load this reference when:** writing or changing tests, adding mocks, or
adding cleanup/helper methods for tests.

## Overview

A test exists to catch a specific break. Two principles govern everything
here:

```
1. Every test names the break it catches
2. Every test exercises the real thing
```

Strict TDD produces both naturally: a test written first and watched
failing against real code has already proven it can fail, and only earns
a mock when the real dependency proves slow or external.

## Principle 1: Name the Break

Before writing the test body, answer: **what production change should
make this test fail — and is that change a bug or a decision?** A test
earns its place by catching a wrong branch, missing side effect, wrong
argument, boundary case, or broken contract.

**Derive expectations independently.** Use literals and hand-checked
fixtures; table-driven tests with literal `want` values are the preferred
shape. An expectation computed by the code under test — or its helpers —
passes no matter what that code does:

```typescript
// ❌ Mirror assertion: the same builder computes both sides — always true
const expected = buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' });
expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe(expected);

// ✅ Hand-derived literal
expect(buildSearchQuery({ tag: 'urgent' })).toBe('tag:"urgent"');
```

**No change detectors.** If only intentional decisions can fail a test —
a constant's value, exact message wording, private structure — it fires
on redesign and sleeps through bugs. Test the behavior that depends on
the decision: not `expect(MAX_RETRIES).toBe(5)` but "a failing call is
retried 5 times and the 6th attempt never happens."

**Behavior, not text.** Asserting that a script, skill, or config
contains an exact line proves only that the source is the source. Run
scripts against controlled inputs and assert outputs, side effects, or
exit codes. Documents that instruct agents are tested by the consuming
agent's behavior (superpowers:writing-skills); prose for humans earns no
test at all.

**Your code, not the framework.** Test the contract your code makes at
its boundaries — the route you register, the query you emit, the payload
you produce. Upstream mechanics are their maintainers' tests to write
(the classic: asserting your router invokes a registered handler — that
is the framework's test, not yours). When upstream behavior genuinely
surprised you, write one narrow characterization test naming the
assumption. The same boundary applies inside your code: constructors,
getters, constants, and trivial forwarding earn tests only when they
validate, normalize, default, derive, enforce, or cause side effects —
otherwise assert the first consumer-visible result that depends on them.

### Gate Function

```
BEFORE writing the test body:
  Name the production change that would make this test fail.

  Cannot name one            → redesign around an observable behavior
  "The source text changed"  → run the artifact and assert its effects
  Only intentional decisions → change detector; test the behavior
                               that depends on the decision

  Confirm the expected value is derived without the code under test.
  IF it reuses the code's logic or helpers:
    Replace it with a literal or hand-checked fixture
```

## Principle 2: Exercise the Real Thing

**The mock earns no assertions.** A mock assertion passes when the mock
is present and fails when it is absent — it says nothing about the
component. Assert the real component's behavior; if the mock is what you
are checking, unmock it or delete the assertion.

```typescript
// ✅ Real behavior
expect(screen.getByRole('navigation')).toBeInTheDocument();

// ❌ Mock existence
expect(screen.getByTestId('sidebar-mock')).toBeInTheDocument();
```

**your human partner's correction:** "Are we testing the behavior of a
mock?"

**Mock at the right level.** Learn every side effect of the real method
before replacing it; mock the slow or external operation and keep what
the test depends on real. When unsure, run the test against the real
implementation first and observe what actually needs to happen.

```typescript
// ❌ The mock swallows the config write that duplicate detection reads
vi.mock('ToolCatalog', () => ({
  discoverAndCacheTools: vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(undefined)
}));

// ✅ Mock only the slow server startup; the config write stays real
vi.mock('MCPServerManager');
```

**Make doubles specific.** When arguments, call counts, or ordering are
part of the contract, assert them — a fake that accepts anything verifies
nothing. Give each branch (success, error, malformed) its own fixture or
spy, so the wrong branch cannot satisfy the expectation.

**Mirror real data completely.** Mock the complete structure as it exists
in reality — all documented fields — not just the ones your test reads.
Partial mocks fail silently when downstream code reads an omitted field:
the test passes while integration breaks.

**Production classes carry production methods only.** Cleanup that only
tests need lives in test utilities, never as a `destroy()` on the
production class. Ask: is this method called only from tests? Does this
class own this resource's lifecycle? Wrong answers → test utility.

**Prefer real components over complex mocks.** When mock setup outgrows
the test logic, mocks miss methods the real components have, or tests
break when the mock changes, switch to an integration test with real
components. **your human partner's question:** "Do we need to be using a
mock here?"

### Gate Function

```
BEFORE adding a mock or test helper:
  List the real method's side effects; keep the ones the test
  depends on real — mock the slow/external level below them.

  Mock responses mirror the complete real structure.

  A method only tests call lives in test utilities, not production.

  About to assert on the mock itself?
    Unmock it or delete the assertion.
```

## Tests Ship With the Implementation

The TDD cycle — failing test, minimal implementation, refactor — is what
"complete" means. Ship the tests the behavior needs and only those:
trivial code and human prose earn none, and a test written to satisfy
process costs maintenance forever.

## The Mutation Check

Before finishing, mentally mutate the production code; at least one test
should fail for each realistic mutation:

- Wrong constant or argument
- Wrong branch handler
- Missing state change or side effect
- Empty or default return
- Missing validation for zero, empty, nil, unauthorized, or malformed input

A mutation nothing catches marks the behavior as unprotected — or the
test as tautological.

## Quick Reference

| When you... | Do |
|-------------|-----|
| Write any test | Name the break it catches — a bug, not a decision |
| Build an expected value | Derive it by hand; never with the code under test |
| Test a script or document | Run it / pressure-test its consumer; never grep its text |
| Reach for a dependency test | Test your boundary contract, not their documented mechanics |
| Want to assert on a mocked element | Test the real component, or unmock it |
| Are about to mock a method | Learn its side effects; mock the slow/external level |
| Build a mock response | Mirror the real structure completely |
| Need cleanup only tests use | Put it in test utilities |
| Watch mock setup balloon | Switch to an integration test with real components |
| Finish a test file | Run the mutation check |

## Warning Signs

- Setup and assertion share the same object, guaranteeing equality
- The test can fail only through a panic, crash, or missing selector
- The test fails on every intentional change, never on accidental breakage
- Expected values are hidden behind loops, builders, or helpers
- The test greps source text, or asserts a removed symbol stays removed
- The test would still matter if only the framework remained
- The test exists for coverage, checking no side effect or outcome
- An assertion checks a `*-mock` test ID, or fails if you remove the mock
- A method is called only from test files
- Mock setup is more than half the test, or you can't explain why the mock is needed
- Mocking "just to be safe"

- **Compose, Don't Inherit**: Build complex things from simple, reusable pieces
- **KISS**: Simple solutions beat clever ones - readable code > smart code
- **Fail Fast**: Throw errors clearly rather than hiding problems with defensive code
- **Extract Early**: See a pattern emerging? Pull it into a shared utility immediately
- **Occam's Razor**: Simplest explanation is usually correct - avoid over-engineering
- **Pareto Principle**: 80% of results come from 20% of effort - focus on high-impact features

<rules>

## Code Quality

- **File Headers**: Every file MUST start with 2-3 sentence comment explaining what it does
- **Strategic Comments**: Comment major sections and complex logic, not every line
- **NO Logging**: MUST NOT use console.log, console.error, or any logging - trust TypeScript and DevTools
- **Progressive Cleanup**: When editing files, replace `any` types with proper interfaces and delete console statements - technical debt decreases over time
- **Real Features**: Build actual functionality - MUST NOT create fake implementations that pretend to be dynamic but return hardcoded results
- **Error Prevention**: Catch problems before they happen, not just handle them
- **Systems Thinking**: Consider how changes affect the bigger picture
- **Zero Technical Debt**: No quick hacks that compromise system integrity

- **Small Files**: Files SHOULD NOT exceed 200 lines; files over 300 lines MUST be split
- **Single Responsibility**: Each file MUST have one clear purpose - if you need "and" to describe it, split it
- **Function Length**: Functions SHOULD NOT exceed 40 lines; extract helpers for complex logic
- **Early Extraction**: When a file approaches 150 lines, proactively identify extraction candidates

## Barrel Exports

- **Index Files**: Every module directory MUST have an `index.ts` barrel file
- **Public API**: Barrel files MUST explicitly export only the public interface - internal helpers stay private

- **Re-export Pattern**: Use `export { ComponentName } from './ComponentName'` - SHOULD NOT use `export *` to keep API explicit
- **Flat Imports**: Barrel exports enable refactoring internals without breaking consumers

## Core Development Rules

1. **Domain Separation** - Organize code by business domain, not technical layers
2. **Configuration Management** - Store configuration in persistent storage; MUST NOT use hardcoded values
3. **Specialized Modules** - Create focused modules for specific business logic
4. **Structured Data Validation** - MUST validate all external data with proper schemas
5. **Pattern Recognition** - Extract common patterns into reusable utilities early
6. **Function Relationships** - Consider how different functions interact and consolidate when patterns emerge
7. **Clean Organization** - Maintain clear directory structure and avoid code sprawl

4. **Edit Precisely**: SHOULD make targeted changes rather than broad rewrites when possible

- **Error Propagation**: Design consistent error handling across all layers

## Type Safety Patterns (Modern Approach)

- **Trust Inference**: Let your type system infer types rather than explicitly typing everything
- **Return Types Sparingly**: Only add explicit return types when they add value or prevent errors
- **Inference > Explicit**: Modern type systems are smarter than manual type annotations
- **Structured Data**: Use strict schemas for API boundaries, flexible types for internal logic

## How OpenCode Manages Plugins

**Users do NOT need to run `npm install`** - OpenCode automatically installs plugin dependencies at runtime.

Users simply add the plugin name to their config:

```jsonc
{
  "plugin": [
    "my-plugin@1.0.0", // Pinned version - won't auto-update
    "another-plugin", // No version = "latest" - updates on launch
  ],
}
```

**On launch, OpenCode:**

1. Runs `bun add --force` for each plugin (auto-installs)
2. Caches pinned versions until user changes config
3. For unpinned plugins, resolves `latest` and caches actual version

This means the README SHOULD NOT include `npm install` instructions - just tell users to add the plugin to their config.

</instructions>

## Common Mistakes

| Mistake                         | Fix                                  |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| Missing `type: "module"`        | Add to package.json                  |
| Not building before publish     | Add `prepublishOnly` script          |
| Wrong main entry                | Point to compiled JS, not TS         |
| Missing @opencode-ai/plugin dep | Add as peerDependency                |

# Testing Plugins

> How to test plugins during development

<workflow>

## Step 1: Create Test Environment

Create a test folder with an `opencode.json` that loads your plugin from source.

### If developing within opencode source folder:

```bash
mkdir -p /path/to/opencode/test-my-plugin
```

```jsonc
// /path/to/opencode/test-my-plugin/opencode.json
{
  "plugin": ["file:///path/to/opencode/.opencode/plugin/my-plugin/index.ts"],
}
```

### If developing in a standalone folder:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/my-plugin-project/test
```

```jsonc
// ~/my-plugin-project/test/opencode.json
{
  "plugin": ["file:///home/user/my-plugin-project/my-plugin/index.ts"],
}
```

The `file://` prefix tells OpenCode to load the plugin directly from source (TypeScript or JavaScript) without requiring npm publish.

## Step 2: Verify Plugin Loads

Run a quick command to verify the plugin initializes without errors:

```bash
cd /path/to/test-folder
opencode run hi
```

This will:

- Start OpenCode
- Load all plugins (including yours)
- Run "hi" prompt
- Exit

**Watch for:**

- Plugin initialization errors in output
- Missing dependencies
- TypeScript compilation errors

## Step 3: Interactive Testing

Run OpenCode interactively in the test folder:

```bash
cd /path/to/test-folder
opencode
```

### Test checklist based on hook type:

| Hook                  | How to Test                                                  |
| --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `event`               | Perform actions that trigger events, check console logs      |
| `tool`                | Ask the LLM to use your custom tool                          |
| `tool.execute.before` | Run the tool being intercepted, verify blocking/modification |
| `tool.execute.after`  | Run tools, check output modifications                        |
| `permission.ask`      | Trigger permission prompts, verify overrides                 |
| `chat.params`         | Check LLM behavior changes (temperature, etc.)               |
| `config`              | Verify config mutations take effect                          |
| `auth`                | Run `/auth` command for your provider                        |

## Step 4: Testing Toasts and UI Feedback

If your plugin shows toasts or inline messages:

1. Trigger the condition that shows the notification
2. Verify toast appears with correct variant/message
3. Check duration is appropriate
4. Test error cases (TUI unavailable) - plugin MUST NOT crash

</workflow>

## Unit Testing (Optional)

For complex plugins, MAY create unit tests with mocked context:

```typescript
// test-plugin.ts
import { MyPlugin } from "./my-plugin"

const mockClient = {
  tui: {
    showToast: async (params: any) => {
      console.log("Toast:", params.body)
      return true
    },
  },
  session: {
    prompt: async (params: any) => {
      console.log("Inline message:", params.body.parts[0].text)
    },
  },
}

const mockContext = {
  project: { id: "test", worktree: "/tmp", time: { created: 0, updated: 0 } },
  client: mockClient as any,
  $: Bun.$ as any,
  directory: "/tmp",
  worktree: "/tmp",
}

const hooks = await MyPlugin(mockContext)

// Test event hook
await hooks.event?.({
  event: { type: "session.idle", properties: { sessionID: "123" } },
})

// Test tool execution hook
await hooks["tool.execute.before"]?.({ tool: "read", sessionID: "123", callID: "abc" }, { args: { filePath: ".env" } })
```

Run with:

```bash
bun run test-plugin.ts
```
